  "text": "## Experiment 4
Experiment 3 demonstrated that positive mood only leads to self-serving responding when the distinctive similarity information is ambiguous. Experiment 4 extends these finding by testing the hypothesis that asymmetric responding in a positive mood results from effortful reinterpretation of ambiguous information, after initial processing leads to detrimental results. To test this hypothesis, participants completed a mood induction exercise, were asked to complete a cognitively effortful task, and then viewed a comparison target with whom they shared a birthday.

As in Experiments 1 and 2, participants were provided with ambiguous similarity information. Reinterpretation of this information was only expected when such reinterpretation was necessary and when individuals had sufficient cognitive resources. Consequently, for participants not under cognitive load, replication of the positive mood conditions from Experiments 1 and 2 was expected. However, for participants under load, replication of the neutral mood conditions from Experiment 2 was expected; lack of cognitive resources was expected to disrupt reinterpretation of ambiguous similarity information, thus preventing participants from responding positively to the downward comparison condition.

## Method

## Participants and design
University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated in the study for monetary compensation. This experiment used a 2(mood: positive, neutral) × 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) × 2(load: load vs. no load) factorial design, with an additional no mood induction, no comparison, no load control condition.

## Procedure
The experimental procedures were the same as in Experiments 1 and 2. As in Experiment 1, participants completed either the happy or neutral mood exercise; there was no negative mood condition. Second, all participants viewed information about an attractive or unattractive comparison target which included information that they shared a birthday with the comparison target. Third, participants in the cognitive load conditions were asked to remember an 8-digit number and to be prepared to report the number when the experiment was finished (see Gilbert, Giesler, and Morris [1995]). Participants were not allowed to write down or otherwise record that number, but were asked to hold it in mind throughout the rest of the study. All participants were able to recall the number at the end of the session. Participants in the no load conditions were not given a number to rehearse.

After viewing the comparison targets, participants then completed the same measures of mood, own attractiveness, and other attractiveness as in Experiments 1 and 2.

## Results and discussion
As in Experiment 2, a hanging control (no load, no mood, no comparison) condition was included in this study and the same analysis strategy was employed. First, a 2(load: load vs. no load) × 2(mood: positive, neutral) × 2 (direction of comparison: upward vs. downward) ANOVA was conducted, testing for main effects and interactions, followed by single degree of freedom contrasts to test specific hypotheses (Jaccard [1998]).

## Manipulation check
As expected, there was a main effect of mood induction on mood, F(1, 124) = 14.94, p < .001. Participants in the positive condition were more positive (M = 5.35, SD = .81) than participants in the neutral condition (M = 4.60, SD = .93). In addition, the attractive comparison target was rated more attractive than the (M = 5.58, SD = .78) than the unattractive target (M = 2.99, SD = .89), F(1,110) = 259.08, p < .001. No other effects on ratings of attractiveness or mood were significant, Fs < 1.

## Self-evaluations
Analysis revealed the expected three-way interaction effect of load, mood, and direction of comparison on attractiveness, F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001. The effects of load, F(1, 110) = 8.00, p = .006; mood F(1, 110) = 9.83, p = .002; direction, F(1, 110) = 135.31, p < .001; load and mood, F(1, 110) = 10.97, p = .001; load and direction, F(1, 110) = 10.44, p = .002 and mood and direction, F(1, 110) = 4.14, p = .04, were also significant.

For ease of interpreting the three-way interaction, the pattern of means is presented in Fig. 3, and the cognitive load and no load conditions are analyzed separately, with comparisons to the control condition.5

## No load conditions
All participants in the study believed they shared a birthday with the comparison targets; therefore, the positive mood conditions were expected to replicate the positive mood and shared-birthday conditions in Experiment 1.

The expected asymmetry among positive mood participants was found. Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found, regardless of whether participants upwardly compared (M = 5.64, SD = .78; F(1,124) = 17.39, p < .001) or downwardly compared (M = 5.15, SD = .81), F(1,124) = 11.90, p = .001.

The neutral mood conditions replicated previous findings of symmetric assimilation (Brown et al. [1992]). Upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.47, SD = .51) than the control condition, F(1,124) = 17.89, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings than the control condition (M = 3.24, SD = 1.09), F(1,124) = 10.37, p = .002.

Thus, positive mood led to asymmetric and self-serving responses, whereas neutral mood led to symmetric responses.

## Cognitive load conditions
Cognitive load was expected to disrupt the self-serving processing of participants in a positive mood, leading them to respond in the same manner as those in the neutral mood conditions.

As expected, cognitive load disrupted the self-serving responding associated with a positive mood. Instead, participants in a positive mood assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Compared to a control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21), upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 5.71, SD = .83), F(1,124) = 23.14, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 3.09, SD = .94), t(124) = -3.30, p = .001. This pattern was identical to the neutral mood condition, in which upward comparison led to more positive self-ratings (M = 3.33, SD = 1.05), F(1,124) = 18.83, p < .001, and downward comparison led to less positive self-ratings (M = 5.53, SD = .87), F(1,124) = 7.84, p = .006, relative to the control condition.

Experiment 4 demonstrated that self-serving responding associated with positive mood is resource-dependent. When people in a positive mood were not under additional cognitive load, they adjusted their interpretations of the meaning of a shared birthday and responded to comparison targets in a self-serving ways, replicating Experiments 1 and 2. However, when cognitive resources were reduced, it was more difficult to adjust the interpretation of the meaning of a shared a birthday and, consequently, participants did not respond to comparisons in self-serving ways. Instead, their responses were like those of neutral mood participants: They assimilated to both upward and downward comparison targets. Thus, when cognitive resources were lacking, the benefits of a positive mood were muted.

## General discussion
In four studies, positive mood led to self-serving interpretations of ambiguous similarity information. When participants were given ambiguous similarity information, they categorized targets in self-serving ways. If the comparison person was superior, they used the information to make the target distinctively similar, basked in that person’s glory, and boosted their self-evaluations. If the comparison person was inferior, they used the information to make the target either irrelevant or only generally similar, leading to no response to the comparison target or contrast of their self-evaluations with the inferior target. Overall, this pattern of self-serving responding was not found when the preference information was unambiguous or when participants were under cognitive loaded.

These studies establish that mood can determine how people interpret and respond to comparison information. These studies also revealed boundary conditions to self-serving responding that provide insight into the underlying processes. First, self-serving responses only occurred when individuals were given ambiguous or flexible information about the relation between themselves and a comparison target. In Experiment 1, when individuals were not told that they shared a birthday with the comparison targets, they were unable to respond in a self-serving manner. Likewise, in Experiment 3, when similarity information was unambiguous, they did not respond in a self-serving manner. Thus, while positive mood might provide cognitive flexibility, positive mood does not blind individuals from seeing negative information. In the absence of ambiguous information, self-serving responses did not arise.

Second, the effect only occurred when individuals had adequate cognitive resources. That cognitive load derailed the self-serving responses suggests that the flexible processing of comparison targets in positive moods is an effortful process and may be a correction process (e.g., Gilbert et al. [1995]; Stapel and Marx [2007]). In Experiment 4, in the absence of adequate cognitive resources, positive mood participants’ responses to the comparison targets were similar to the responses to neutral mood participants. That is, they were unable to make corrections or engage in reinterpretation of ambiguous information in order to avoid assimilation to the downward comparison target. This supports our suggestion of a two-step process in which individuals in a positive mood initially respond to social comparison information in a consistent manner, and only engage in effortful reanalysis of ambiguous information in order to correct for the negative influence of social comparison.

In addition, this finding contradicts an alternative explanation that our effects are the result of positive moods inducing heuristic processing and negative moods inducing systematic processing. If heuristic processing were responsible for how participants responded to the comparisons, we would expect the same level of processing of both upward and downward comparisons, with symmetric contrast (or assimilation) to both types of targets. However, positive moods led to the use of a trivial similarity cue to indicate similarity in the upward comparison condition but not in the downward comparison conditions. In addition, if heuristic processing were responsible for the effects in the positive mood conditions, then inducing cognitive load should not have eliminated the self-serving pattern.

Third, we found asymmetry only under positive mood, not under negative mood. If self-serving responses were only defensive, we might have found that negative mood, an aversive state, would have led to an interpretation of information that allowed for recovery. Alternatively, if responses resulted from mood-congruent information search and processing, we would expect that negative mood should lead to asymmetrically negative responses. Instead, negative mood was associated with processing of information with greater neutrality, objectivity, and focus on the data at hand, regardless of the consequence for self-evaluations (for reviews see Bless [2001]; Martin and Clore [2001]).

Finally, the results of the present studies suggest that asymmetric responses are not a result of using mood as a resource (Trope et al. [2001]). According to this model, a positive mood can be a treated as resource to be expended in the pursuit of accurate information. If this were true, in this case, we would have expected that positive mood would have been associated with contrastive responses to comparison targets, a response that is associated with information-seeking motives (Stapel and Koomen [2001a]). Indeed, in other research, the experience of self-affirmation is related to just such symmetric responses to comparisons (Johnson and Stapel, in press).

In sum, these findings support the growing body of literature showing that positive moods can create an upward spiral (Fredrickson and Joiner [2002]). Numerous cognitive processes are associated with positive mood and in responding to social comparison information; among these the ability to make fine distinctions between distinctive similarity and general similarity may be particularly helpful. Individuals in a positive mood were able to convert what could be considered negative feedback (one is less attractive than another person) into positive self-evaluations. Positive mood granted individuals the ability to see a shared-birthday or a shared-artistic preference as meaningful indicators of shared distinctiveness and similarity, allowing them to assimilate to upward comparison targets. Positive mood also granted individuals the ability to recognize a shared-birthday a meaningless indicator of similarity, and allowed them to contrast with downward comparison targets.

Future research might investigate how dispositional happiness might be related to the self-serving bias presented here. If positive emotions do create an upward spiral, consistently interpreting ambiguity in self-serving ways might one way in which dispostionally happy people are able to reap self-evaluative boosts from downward comparisons and are buffered from the self-depreciating effects of upward comparisons (Lyubomirsky and Ross [1997]).

## Conclusions
It has become increasingly clear that while social comparisons may be ubiquitous, the impact of social comparison information is highly dependent upon the contexts within which comparisons arise and the motivations of the individuals involved. The present studies add to the existing literature by highlighting how mood can influence how individuals treat similarity cues in their environment, such as social comparison information. In the presence of a positive mood, ambiguous social comparison information is interpreted in a self-serving manner, such that positive self-evaluations result. Thus, a good mood can beget not only a good mood, but also beget a more positive self-image.

headline.statement: A reported significance test in Experiment 1 uses more degrees of freedom than the paper's own stated sample size can produce -- the analysis it presents could not have been run on the sample it describes.
headline.evidence: "Female university (N = 47) students participated in the study for monetary compensation" and, for the contrast in question, "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" -- an error (denominator) degrees of freedom of 46. For any two-group comparison drawn from a fixed total sample, the maximum attainable error df is N-2; with the paper's own N=47 that ceiling is 45, one less than what is printed. The same experiment's other, larger 2x2 model already uses df=43 (e.g. F(1,43)=38.80), which is itself the largest df available from a 4-cell split of 47 participants -- so the single two-cell contrast cannot legitimately carry a larger df than the four-cell omnibus model.
headline.plain: The researchers describe recruiting 47 women for this study. But one of their key statistical tests reports using more "degrees of freedom" than 47 people can supply -- roughly speaking, the test claims to have compared more people than were ever in the room. The underlying p-value is fine on its own terms, but the sample size behind it is not real.

findings.title: Denominator degrees of freedom (df=46) exceeds the paper's own stated sample size (N=47)
findings.reported: "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" for the contrast between upward and downward comparison targets, in the unshared-birthday subset of a study explicitly described as "Female university (N = 47) students."
findings.computed: For any independent two-group split of a fixed total sample, maximum attainable error df = N-2. With the paper's own stated N=47, that ceiling is 45 -- one less than the printed df=46, and less than the 46 minimum participants (df+2) the printed value would require. The same experiment's own 4-cell 2x2 omnibus model (the largest model the design supports) uses df=43 throughout (F(1,43)=38.80; F(1,43)=7.77; F(1,43)=5.99) -- consistent with N=47 minus 4 cells -- so this single two-group contrast, drawn from at most half the sample, cannot legitimately exceed even that larger model's df, let alone the absolute N-2 ceiling. Re-running the F-to-p conversion (F=6.95, df1=1, df2=46) confirms the printed p=.011 is internally consistent with the printed F and df -- the arithmetic of the p-value is not the problem; the problem is that df=46 cannot have come from this sample.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own stated N=47 for Experiment 1 and the logically necessary bound df<=N-2 for any two-group comparison drawn from a fixed sample; no invented range or scale is used.
findings.plain: One of the paper's central results -- that participants who did not share a birthday with a comparison target responded symmetrically, the finding used to argue that ambiguous similarity information is necessary for the self-serving effect -- reports a statistical test drawn from more people than the study says it recruited. This is not a rounding slip; it is a number that cannot come from the sample as described, which means a reader cannot verify what test was actually run or trust the result attached to it.

consequence.explanation: This is the specific contrast supporting the paper's claim that self-serving responding requires ambiguous similarity information (Hypothesis 1, stated as a primary result). The printed p-value cannot be traced to a real sample, so this piece of evidence for the paper's central claim cannot be verified.

findings.title: Identical denominator df (124) recurs across four unrelated subgroup breakdowns in two different experiments with different total sample sizes
findings.location: Experiment 2 (Positive mood and Negative mood sections, N=141) and Experiment 4 (No load and Cognitive load sections, N=193)
findings.reported: Experiment 2: "in the positive mood conditions, direction of comparison, F(1, 124) = 14.79"; "presence of similarity cue... F(1, 124) = 18.61"; "interaction effect of direction of comparison and similarity information, F(1, 124) = 9.39"; and separately, "Among the negative mood conditions, only the main effect of direction was significant, F(1, 124) = 56.97." Experiment 4: "F(1,124) = 17.39"; "F(1,124) = 11.90"; "F(1,124) = 17.89"; "F(1,124) = 10.37"; "F(1,124) = 23.14"; "t(124) = -3.30"; "F(1,124) = 18.83"; "F(1,124) = 7.84."
findings.computed: Experiment 2's own internally consistent models establish a factorial-only sample of N=126 (the paper's df=118 omnibus model on the full 8-cell design implies N_factorial-8=118, i.e. N=126, leaving a control n of 15 against the total N=141 and its df=132 nine-condition model). The positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only subgroup tests, each drawn from a subset of that same 126-person factorial pool, both report the identical residual df=124 -- which, on a 2(direction)x2(cue) model (4 parameters), implies a subgroup n of 128 for EACH mood group. Two subgroups of 128 people cannot both be drawn from a shared pool of 126: even a single subgroup of 128 already exceeds the entire factorial sample. The identical value 124 is then reused, unexplained, for eight further tests across a wholly different experiment (Experiment 4, total N=193, its own factorial-only omnibus using df=110).
findings.assumptions: Assumes the positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only tests use a standard multi-parameter ANOVA model (direction x cue) rather than an undocumented pooled-error contrast scheme; the paper does state it used single-df pooled contrasts (citing Jaccard 1998) for its explicit control-condition comparisons (the F(1,132)/F(1,132) tests), so an unreported variant of that same pooling scheme applied instead to these mood-subset breakdowns cannot be entirely ruled out, which is why this stops short of impossible.
findings.plain: The number of participants behind a statistical test is supposed to change when you change the group being tested. Here, the exact same denominator (124) appears for a breakdown of positive-mood participants and, separately, for a breakdown of negative-mood participants in the same experiment -- and then again for entirely different breakdowns in an unrelated experiment with a different total number of participants. Under the sample sizes the paper itself reports elsewhere, this value cannot arise honestly from either subgroup. This bears directly on the tests that support three of the paper's four central hypotheses.

findings.title: Two significant p-values print without their leading decimal point
findings.reported: "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" and "F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001" (both missing the leading decimal that would read p = .011 and p = .001).
findings.computed: Recalculating F(1,46)=6.95 gives p=.0114, consistent with the intended .011 reading; the second instance sits alongside a df already found to be irreconcilable with the paper's stated N (see rank 1). Both are typesetting defects rather than arithmetic errors on their own.
findings.assumptions: None beyond ordinary APA decimal notation; treated as a proofreading slip, not a computational one.
findings.plain: Two of the paper's reported p-values are missing their decimal point (printed as "011" instead of ".011"). Read the intended way, the numbers are fine. On its own this is an ordinary proofreading slip -- but one of the two sentences it appears in is also the sentence carrying the impossible degrees-of-freedom problem above, which is worth noting even though it proves nothing by itself.

findings.title: No table or experiment reports per-cell sample sizes, blocking GRIM/GRIMMER verification of every mean and SD
findings.location: Table 1 (Experiment 2, 8 cells) and Table 2 (Experiment 3, 16 cells); all four experiments generally
findings.reported: Both tables print mean (SD) on stated, printable scales (a single seven-point self-evaluation item; a three-item nine-point similarity composite), but neither the tables nor the surrounding text state a per-cell or per-condition n anywhere in the paper -- only total experiment N and various ANOVA error degrees of freedom.
findings.computed: check_table was run against both tables' 24 mean/SD cells; grim_check, grimmer_check and sprite_reconstruct all refused for want of a per-cell n, which error df alone cannot supply without assuming perfectly balanced cells (an assumption the instructions direct against making).
findings.assumptions: None -- this is a refusal to check, not a finding about the numbers themselves.
findings.plain: The paper's two summary tables report averages and spreads for each experimental group, but never say how many people were in each group -- only the total for the whole experiment. That gap means the paper's most checkable numbers (the individual cell means) cannot be verified at all, in either direction. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of a problem with the numbers themselves.

not_checked.reason: No per-cell or per-condition sample size is reported anywhere in the paper, so GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE cannot be run on these stated-scale (1-7) single-item means without assuming an unstated per-cell n.
Same missing-per-cell-n limitation as Table 1. The Similarity row is additionally a 3-item composite mean, which this toolkit's GRIM/GRIMMER cannot correctly evaluate even with n known.

not_checked.location: Pilot study mood and self-evaluation composite indices
not_checked.reason: Both are multi-item composite means (4 items; 3 items); this toolkit's granularity checks model single-item integer data, not k-item composites, and per-group n is not reported either.

No experiment reports the number of participants in each factorial cell; only total N and various ANOVA error degrees of freedom are given, which do not determine individual cell sizes without assuming balance.

not_checked.location: Pairwise p-values reported only as thresholds (e.g. 'p < .001', 'ps > .84')
not_checked.reason: A large share of the paper's p-values are reported only as bounds without an exact value or accompanying test statistic sufficient for further recomputation.

limitations: Figures were not read in this stage; Stage 1 examined all three figures with extract_figures and found none carries a numeric value not already printed in the text or tables, and that finding is carried forward here without independent re-verification of the images.

Three findings in the Stage-1 sweep were initially flagged by the automated second-look worklist as 'quote not located.' On re-reading the source XML directly (rather than relying on a possibly non-contiguous composited quote), all three underlying passages were located verbatim in the paper; the marker fired because the sweep's quotes joined non-adjacent sentences with ellipses rather than because the values were misread. This is recorded once here rather than three times.

No per-cell or per-condition sample sizes are reported anywhere in this paper, which blocks GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE verification of every individual mean and SD in Tables 1 and 2 -- the paper's most granular, and otherwise most checkable, numbers.

This paper carries a journal-issued retraction header and is one of the works covered by the Levelt Committee's finding of fabricated data by co-author Diederik Stapel; that background is noted for context but is not itself evidence for any specific finding above, each of which rests on the paper's own printed numbers.

R cross-checks were not applicable here: no GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE finding was produced by the sweep (the paper's stated scales support these checks in principle, but the missing per-cell n blocks them, per the indeterminate finding above), so the r_grim_ground_truth / r_sprite_ground_truth cross-check requirement did not apply to any finding in this report.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you supply the exact analytic model (including the number of participants) used for the F(1, 46) = 6.95 contrast in Experiment 1's unshared-birthday self-evaluations, and separately for the F(1, 124) tests reported in Experiment 2's positive-mood and negative-mood sections and in Experiment 4's no-load and cognitive-load sections?
questions_for_authors.why: These denominator degrees of freedom cannot be reconciled with the paper's own stated total sample sizes under a standard ANOVA model; the authors' underlying dataset or analysis code, if available, would settle whether an unreported pooled-error or contrast specification explains the values.

input.report_markdown:
This paper reports a pilot study and four between-subjects lab experiments (total participants across studies: 45, 47, 141, 96, 193) arguing that positive mood leads people to interpret ambiguous social-comparison information in self-serving ways -- assimilating toward better-off comparison targets and contrasting away from worse-off ones -- while negative mood and unambiguous information do not produce this pattern. The paper was later retracted; it is one of the works covered by the Levelt Committee's finding that co-author Diederik Stapel fabricated data across a large body of his published work. That history is background, not evidence, and every finding below rests on the paper's own printed numbers rather than on that history.

Sixty-three NHST statistics were recovered from the text and run through statcheck; none showed a decision-changing gap between a printed test statistic and its printed p-value. Several individual F-to-p recalculations (the pilot's F(1,42)=.27/p=.76, Experiment 3's F(1,94)=1.50/p=.83, and others) turned up sizeable but non-decision-changing gaps -- each an under-claim, where the true p implied by the statistic is smaller and more significant than what was printed, the conservative direction rather than the inflating one. Two families of planned control contrasts (four tests in Experiment 2, eight in Experiment 4) were checked for multiplicity and none loses significance under any of four standard corrections. As far as this class of check goes, the paper's arithmetic is largely unremarkable.

The problem is elsewhere, in the bookkeeping behind the degrees of freedom themselves. Experiment 1 states plainly that 47 women took part, and its main 2x2 model consistently uses an error df of 43 -- exactly what a four-cell split of 47 participants supports. But the one contrast that anchors the paper's headline claim about Experiment 1 (that responses are symmetric, not self-serving, when similarity information is absent) reports F(1, 46) = 6.95: an error df of 46, one more than even the full sample's own two-group ceiling of 45, and three more than the four-cell model's own df of 43. The p-value that goes with it is internally correct for the printed F and df -- this is not a p-value error -- but the degrees of freedom cannot have come from this sample under any partition of it.

That is bad enough to be the headline on its own. It is not the only instance of the pattern. The identical value 124 recurs as the denominator df for four different subgroup breakdowns split across two experiments with different total sample sizes -- positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only tests in Experiment 2 (N=141), and no-load and cognitive-load tests in Experiment 4 (N=193). Experiment 2's own internally consistent numbers pin its factorial-only sample at 126 participants; a positive-mood-only 2x2 test with df=124 implies a subgroup of 128 people, which alone exceeds the entire 126-person factorial pool, before even asking where the negative-mood participants (needed for the parallel df=124 test reported two paragraphs later) would come from. I have stopped short of calling this impossible outright, because the paper does describe using an unreported pooled single-degree-of-freedom contrast method (citing Jaccard 1998) for some of its comparisons, and I cannot fully rule out an undocumented variant of that scheme producing this number by a route I have not reconstructed. But every ordinary reading of the reported model fails, and the same failure recurring identically across two unrelated experiments is not the kind of thing honest rounding or typesetting produces.

A minor, lower-stakes observation: two of the paper's p-values print without their decimal point ("p = 011" and "p = 001" rather than ".011" and ".001"). Read the intended way the arithmetic checks out, so this is recorded as an ordinary proofreading slip -- worth noting only because one of the two sentences carrying it is the same sentence carrying the impossible-df problem above.

Finally, neither of the paper's two data tables, nor any of its four experiments, reports how many participants sat in each experimental cell -- only the total N per experiment and various omnibus error degrees of freedom. That gap makes it impossible to run GRIM, GRIMMER, or SPRITE on any of the paper's individual cell means, which are otherwise exactly the kind of stated-scale, small-Likert data those checks are built for. This is recorded as a reporting gap rather than a finding about the numbers themselves, but it means the paper's most granular claims are simply not checkable from what it printed.

I do not have confidence that the reported statistics in Experiment 1 and the positive/negative-mood breakdowns of Experiment 2 and Experiment 4 come from the samples the paper describes.
